failing_part: "are randomForest's/ranger's defaults" (mtry max(floor(p/3),1) for a number; smallest leaf 10 for class probabilities)
narrowest_regime: Each value is a default of one package, not of either: classification mtry floor(sqrt(p)) is both packages'; the p/3 regression mtry is randomForest only; the 10 for probability forests is ranger's probability-forest min.node.size only. Bagging remark about sklearn's regressor (max_features=1.0) is right.
reason: randomForest: ntree 500, mtry sqrt(p) / max(floor(p/3),1), nodesize 1 (class) / 5 (regression). ranger: num.trees 500, mtry floor(sqrt(p)) for ALL types including regression, min.node.size 1 / 5 / 3 / 10 (probability). So the stated set is a hybrid of the two packages, and both packages' node sizes are split thresholds (nodes smaller than the value are not split), not minimum leaf sizes; min leaf 10 (each child >= 10) is stricter, which the claim concedes only for the class case and which is also true for the 5 on numbers. The settings are reasonable defaults and the 'bagging' contrast with sklearn's regressor is correct, so the error is one of attribution, not of method.

citations.cite: ranger R documentation (num.trees 500; mtry floor(sqrt(p)) for all types; min.node.size 1/5/3/10 by type, 'minimal node size to split at')
randomForest R documentation (ntree 500; mtry sqrt(p) or max(floor(p/3),1); nodesize 1 class / 5 regression)
Probst, Wright & Boulesteix 2019, WIREs Data Mining Knowl Discov, Hyperparameters and tuning strategies for random forest
Liaw & Wiener 2002, R News 2:18-22

bite_note: Using mtry=p/3 and min leaf 5/10 instead of scikit-learn's regressor default (bagging, max_features=1.0) changes fits, modestly; the misattribution itself changes no result, only how the default is defended.

failing_part: "more of that nutrient in place of the same energy from the energy sources not in the model ... not the effect of simply eating more of it" applied to every nutrient exposure
narrowest_regime: Energy-yielding exposures (carbohydrate, fat, protein, alcohol or their fractions) in a linear model with no effect modification, causal reading under the usual no-unmeasured-confounding assumptions. For a non-energy nutrient (vitamin, mineral, sodium) nothing is substituted: the coefficient is the contrast at fixed total energy, which is 'more of it' with the energy sources unchanged.
reason: For a macronutrient the standard model (nutrient + total energy) and the residual model with energy kept are reparametrisations, so the nutrient coefficient is a substitution for the energy sources left out, and with several sources in the model 'everything else' is only the omitted ones; this matches Tomova et al. 2022. The claim is stated for 'nutrient exposures' and is used to read 'every energy-adjusted coefficient', but for a nutrient that contributes no energy there is no source to displace, so the substitution gloss is wrong for it.

citations.cite: Tomova GD, Arnold KF, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG 2022, Adjustment for energy intake in nutritional research: a causal inference perspective, Am J Clin Nutr (PMID 34313676); abstract says standard and residual models estimate a substitution effect
Tomova GD, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PW 2022, Theory and performance of substitution models for estimating relative causal effects in nutritional epidemiology, Am J Clin Nutr (PMID 36223891)
Willett & Stampfer 1986, Am J Epidemiol 124:17-27

bite_note: Changes how a micronutrient's energy-adjusted coefficient is captioned and read; for macronutrients the reading is right and drives how researchers state their estimand.

narrowest_regime: Stated regime; the claim is hedged ('can be', 'plausibly') and holds as a causal-structure warning for adiposity-type outcomes.
reason: Diet composition -> true energy -> adiposity makes energy a mediator, so adjusting blocks the energy-mediated part of a total effect; reported energy is a child of true energy and of adiposity (under-reporting rises with adiposity), so conditioning on it opens nutrient -> true energy -> reported energy <- adiposity, a collider path. Both problems can operate together, and showing the adjusted (substitution) and unadjusted (total/additive) models is a reasonable sensitivity presentation. The warning does not say adjustment is always wrong: for the substitution estimand the energy-adjusted model is intended.

citations.cite: Tomova et al. 2022 Am J Clin Nutr 115:189 (energy as mediator/confounder in DAGs)
Livingstone & Black 2003, J Nutr 133:895S (BMI-related under-reporting of energy)

bite_note: Triggers a DISPUTED flag and prompts presenting both adjusted and unadjusted models for BMI/diabetes-type outcomes, instead of reporting the energy-adjusted coefficient alone.

narrowest_regime: When the product is a probability, mean or class-probability prediction scored by a proper loss; 'never' AUC would be too strong only if the sole deployment use were ranking.
reason: Pooled sum(w*loss)/sum(w) over all inner validation rows is the CV estimate of the expected proper loss; it differs from the average of per-fold mean losses only by fold weights, and per-fold R-squared adds a fold-specific denominator that makes the criterion unstable. AUC and accuracy ignore calibration or are discontinuous, so they pick less shrinkage than the proper loss wants. In a simulation (ridge logistic, n=150, p=30, 40 reps) tuning C by CV AUC gave test log loss 0.666 and by accuracy 0.641 versus 0.610 for tuning on pooled log loss (differences 0.056 and 0.031, 5 and 4 standard errors).

citations.cite: Gneiting & Raftery 2007, JASA 102:359, Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction and estimation
own simulation work_11_sonnet/tune_obj.py

bite_note: Moving from scikit-learn's default scoring (accuracy / mean per-fold R-squared) or AUC to pooled proper loss changes the selected penalty and worsens/improves test log loss by about 0.03 to 0.06 in the simulated regime; pooled-versus-per-fold-mean for MSE by itself changes little.

failing_part: "needs at least 100 held-out rows ... to be useful" as a threshold
narrowest_regime: As a conservative convention for ordering options (small n favours cross-validation over a single 20% holdout); not as a derived minimum.
reason: The 100-events-and-100-non-events figure for binary outcomes came from resampling studies of c-index and calibration, and later work argues that required validation size depends on the target precision of each measure and the outcome distribution, so no fixed count transfers. For a continuous outcome, the relative standard error of a held-out MSE is about sqrt((kurtosis-1)/n), about 14% at n=100 with normal errors (7% for RMSE); whether that is useful depends on the decision, so 100 is invented precision. The direction is sound: single small holdouts are noisy and cross-validation uses all rows (the claim itself calls it a convention with no citation).

citations.cite: Collins GS, Ogundimu EO, Altman DG 2016, Stat Med 35:214, Sample size considerations for the external validation of a multivariable prognostic model: a resampling study (min. 100 events, ideally 200+)
Riley RD et al. 2024, BMJ, Evaluation of clinical prediction models (part 3): calculating the sample size required for an external validation study
Vergouwe Y et al. 2005, J Clin Epidemiol 58:475

bite_note: Reorders the split question for continuous/multiclass outcomes with a 20% holdout below the floor (roughly n < 500), so cross-validation is offered first; the user can still choose either.

failing_part: "is narrower than the distribution of usual intake ... percentiles read from it understate the share in both tails"
narrowest_regime: Nowhere: the mean of two recalls is narrower than a single recall's distribution but wider than the usual-intake distribution.
reason: Observed two-day mean = usual intake + mean of within-person day-to-day deviations, so its variance is sigma_b^2 + sigma_w^2/2, larger than sigma_b^2 for usual intake. Averaging lowers the inflation relative to one day but does not remove it, and a person's own mean is not pulled toward the population mean (that shrinkage is what the NCI/ISU methods apply to correct this). Percentiles of the two-day-mean distribution therefore overstate the shares in both tails, the opposite of the claim; with sigma_w^2/sigma_b^2 = 2 the SD is about 41% too large.

citations.cite: Tooze JA et al. 2006, J Am Diet Assoc 106:1575-1587
Nusser SM et al. 1996, JASA 91:1440 (ISU method)

bite_note: Reading tail percentiles (e.g. share below EAR or above UL) off observed means would be told to expect understated tails when they are in fact overstated; leads to the wrong direction of correction.

failing_part: "Including the outcome in the imputation model is invalid under every goal, including estimating a regression coefficient ... bias the coefficients away from zero; blanks in predictors must always be imputed without the outcome"
narrowest_regime: Only a prediction model whose imputation at deployment cannot use the outcome (then development-time imputation should mimic deployment, and in-fold leakage must be avoided); for estimating a regression coefficient the outcome must be in the imputation model.
reason: Standard multiple-imputation theory requires the imputation model to include the analysis-model variables, outcome included; leaving it out makes imputed predictor values independent of the outcome given the others and attenuates the coefficient toward zero. In a simulation (y = 0.5 x1 + 0.5 x2 + e, x2 40% missing, 10 stochastic-regression imputations, 300 reps) pooled beta2 was 0.299 without the outcome (beta1 0.615) and 0.498 with it (beta1 0.502); the null coefficient showed no bias away from zero either way. The claimed mechanism (bias away from zero) is the reverse of what happens.

citations.cite: Moons KGM et al. 2006, J Clin Epidemiol 59:1092, Using the outcome for imputation of missing predictor values was preferred

Sisk R et al. 2023, Stat Methods Med Res, Imputation and missing indicators for handling missing data in the development and deployment of clinical prediction models (concerns prediction deployment, not coefficient estimation)
own simulation work_11_sonnet/mi_outcome.py

bite_note: Refusing outcome-informed imputation under the estimate goal would hand the researcher attenuated, biased coefficients and p-values; the natural alternative (include y) is unbiased.

narrowest_regime: Stated regime: binary outcome, marginal RD/RR declared, standardised risks available.
reason: The E-value is defined on the risk-ratio scale; a risk difference carries no E-value without the underlying risks (the same dependence appears in the evalues.RD interface, which takes cell counts), so computing it from the standardised marginal risks as a RR, with the bootstrap limit nearer the null, bounds the declared estimand directly. Applying it to a conditional OR needs the rare-outcome or sqrt(OR) approximation, which is avoidable here. VanderWeele and Ding recommend reporting it for the point estimate and the limit nearest the null.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ & Ding P 2017, Ann Intern Med 167:268-274, Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value

bite_note: For a common outcome the conditional-OR E-value (approximate) and the marginal-RR E-value differ materially, and the declared estimand is the marginal measure.

narrowest_regime: Stated regime. The caps (n/4 levels, at most two candidates) are engineering conventions with no methods derivation but are not presented as more than guesses.
reason: The core assertion holds: injection order and analytical batch are properties of the run, not recoverable from column values, since sample numbers are all-distinct and preparation plates or study groups also form contiguous blocks. A guess-and-confirm design with a 'one curve over the whole run' alternative is a sound response, and the rule excluding one-row levels keeps order-like columns out of batch candidates. The thresholds are unjustified conventions but do not change correctness because the user's choice settles the assignment.

citations.cite: Dunn WB et al. 2011, Nat Protoc 6:1060, QC-RLSC procedure

bite_note: Asking instead of auto-assigning order/batch avoids fitting LOESS drift curves on the wrong order or across true batch boundaries, which would distort feature values.

narrowest_regime: Maximum likelihood exists (no separation) and the solver actually reaches it; exact for Newton/IRLS, not for first-order optimisers with a stopping tolerance at very different column scales.
reason: The logistic likelihood depends on x only through x'beta, so multiplying a column by c>0 maps the MLE to beta/c and leaves fitted and out-of-fold probabilities unchanged. In a check with scaled columns, statsmodels Newton gave identical out-of-fold probabilities (max diff 2e-16 at scale 1e6), while scikit-learn lbfgs without penalty moved by 0.02 at scale 1e3 and 0.37 at 1e6, so not rescaling is safe only with a scale-invariant or well-converged solver.

citations.cite: McCullagh & Nelder 1989, Generalized Linear Models, 2nd ed.
own simulation work_11_sonnet/logit_scale.py

bite_note: With a converged MLE, rescaling cannot change the predictions, so skipping it changes nothing; the only live risk is solver convergence on extreme scales.

narrowest_regime: Stated regime; with m=5 the pooled degrees of freedom should use the Barnard-Rubin small-sample adjustment and design-based df, which the claim does not contradict.
reason: Analysing each completed dataset separately and combining by Rubin's rules (mean of estimates; total variance = within + (1+1/m) between) carries the imputation uncertainty, which is how NCHS instructs users of the five NHANES DXA imputations. Stacking the copies as independent rows would shrink standard errors and ignore between-imputation variance.

citations.cite: Schenker N et al. 2011, Stat Med 30:260, Multiple imputation of missing dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry data in NHANES
Rubin DB 1987, Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys

bite_note: Compared with treating the copies as extra rows, it changes the standard errors and intervals the researcher reports.

narrowest_regime: Stated regime. Unsupervised steps (scaling, outcome-free imputation, PCA) leak far less than supervised ones, but fitting every learned step in-fold is the safe rule.
reason: Any step that uses the held-out rows or labels outside the training fold contaminates the error estimate; supervised feature selection on all samples is the extreme case and with p >> n and no signal can give near-zero apparent error, as shown by Ambroise and McLachlan. Resampling the whole pipeline (including tuning, thresholds, imputation) is the standard internal-validation requirement; the unsupervised-leakage literature finds those effects smaller but nonzero.

citations.cite: Ambroise C & McLachlan GJ 2002, PNAS 99:6562, Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data
Hornung R, Bernau C, Truntzer C et al. 2015, Full versus incomplete cross-validation
Moscovich A & Rosset S 2022, JRSSB, On the cross-validation bias due to unsupervised preprocessing

bite_note: Doing selection or supervised preprocessing before the split can turn a noise-only table into near-zero reported error; in-fold fitting changes the reported performance.
